disease_info: Specific Phobia is characterized by a persistent, excessive fear focused on a clearly identifiable object or situation (e.g., animals, heights, flying, blood/injury) that is out of proportion to the actual threat. The feared stimulus almost invariably elicits an immediate fear or anxiety response and is either avoided or endured with marked distress, typically lasting at least six months and causing significant interference in social, occupational, or other important areas of functioning. Unlike more generalized anxiety disorders, the fear in Specific Phobia is circumscribed rather than pervasive and is not better explained by other conditions such as OCD, PTSD, or social anxiety disorder. Onset often occurs in childhood but can emerge or re-emerge later in life after a triggering event or increased exposure, and many individuals present only when avoidance begins to conflict with key responsibilities or valued activities.

narrative.stressor: About a year ago, Norman was overseeing a multi-story renovation in Springfield when a scaffolding plank gave way under a subcontractor; the worker was caught by his harness and only suffered minor injuries, but Norman was close by and watched the near fall from an upper level. In the weeks that followed, his long-standing but manageable discomfort with heights, which had never interfered with his career or hunting trips in the Ozark foothills, became increasingly intrusive whenever he had to climb ladders, inspect roofs, or walk open framing. As his company picked up more multi-story and light-commercial jobs, he found himself delegating critical site walks, delaying inspections, and arguing with his boss about reassigning him to lower-rise projects, which strained his reputation for being hands-on and competitive with deadlines. When a major contract required him to personally sign off on a rooftop mechanical install and he could not bring himself to complete the inspection despite multiple attempts, his employer suggested he talk to a professional; his wife echoed the concern after noticing how much he was reorganizing his fishing, firefighting, and volunteer water-rescue duties to avoid similar situations, prompting him to seek psychiatric evaluation.
narrative.chief_complaint: I’ve started going out of my way to avoid any job that involves getting up high, and when I can’t avoid it I’m barely able to stay up there long enough to do my work.

narrative.stressor: Roughly thirteen months ago, Kayla slipped on an icy curb in her school’s parking lot and fractured her wrist, an incident that required a brief ER visit but no surgery. Although she healed physically and returned to teaching on schedule, the fall crystallized a long-standing but minor discomfort with hospitals and medical procedures into a much more pronounced dread of anything involving doctors’ offices, imaging suites, or invasive tests. Over the subsequent school year, as her chronic back issues began to flare from long hours at her desk and in the classroom, she repeatedly postponed recommended diagnostic appointments and physical therapy because planning those visits into her otherwise meticulously organized life became a source of escalating internal conflict and distress. When she ultimately canceled a long-awaited spine specialist consultation that she herself had pushed for, and her primary care physician warned her about the risks of continued delay and suggested that her avoidance might be anxiety-based, she reluctantly agreed to a mental health referral to understand why she was going to such lengths to stay away from medical settings.
narrative.chief_complaint: I know it doesn’t make sense, but the thought of going into any kind of medical office or having tests done scares me so much that I keep putting off appointments I really need.

narrative.stressor: About a year and a month ago, Thadeus was riding the bus home from the Oakland Museum when another passenger had a sudden seizure and collapsed in the aisle; the driver pulled over, bystanders called 911, and paramedics crowded the small space to provide care. Though the man ultimately recovered, the chaotic scene and the sight of the medical equipment being used in close quarters left a strong impression on Thadeus, who had previously taken buses and BART trains all over the Bay Area without a second thought. Since then, he has gradually cut back on using public transit, rearranging his docent shifts, missing a few seniors running club meet-ups at Lake Merritt, and turning down invitations to evening jazz sets that would require a bus ride, instead insisting on rides from friends or skipping events altogether. When his primary care clinic noticed he was canceling in-person appointments that required a bus trip and a social worker from a community program visited to check on him, he admitted that it had become increasingly hard to even think about getting on a crowded bus without feeling overwhelmed, and she encouraged him to see a mental health provider.
narrative.chief_complaint: Whenever I even think about getting on a city bus now, I tense up right away and feel like I just can’t go through with the ride.
